novedades.texto: Definitions by society: ACOG PB 217 / NICE / FIGO: rupture of membranes before the onset of labor; preterm (PPROM) if before 37 0/7 wk. FASGO consensus: at least 2 h before the onset of labor. Colombian guideline (2015): more than 1 h before the onset of labor. Latency: time from rupture to the onset of labor. Prolonged PROM: more than 24 h. Epidemiology: PPROM in 2-3% of pregnancies and term PROM in 8% (ACOG PB 217). Periviability: 20 0/7-25 6/7 wk. Survival to discharge: 23 wk 23-27%, 24 wk 42-59%, 25 wk 67-76% (ACOG/SMFM OCC No. 6, 2017; data from the USA, England and Australia before 2017). Tabla propia CaVeSal® · Based on: ACOG PB 217 (2020) · FASGO consensus (2018; 2022 update) · Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol 2015;66(4) · ACOG/SMFM OCC No. 6 (2017). Clinical: clear fluid leaking from the vagina — reliability >90% if visualized at the external cervical os on speculum examination. Confirmatory tests: Fern test. Nitrazine test (pH>6.5 turns blue). Biomarkers: PAMG-1 (AmniSure) is the reference non-invasive test in equivocal cases, owing to its higher specificity; IGFBP-1 + AFP (AmnioQuick Duo+) has comparable accuracy; IGFBP-1 (Actim PROM). Interpret together with the clinical assessment. Measurement of urea and creatinine in vaginal secretions — urea 94%/82% and creatinine 98%/90% (sensitivity/specificity, Alao 2023); low cost, useful in resource-limited settings. See comparative table in subcard 7. Adjunct test: cutoffs not standardized; not adopted by ACOG, RCOG, NICE or FIGO guidelines. Amniocentesis: now reserved for selected cases because it is invasive. Uses: (1) definitive diagnosis of PROM with indigo carmine or fluorescein (vaginal tampon, check staining at 20-60 min); (2) subclinical intra-amniotic infection (20-34 wk): glucose, Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic and mycoplasma cultures; (3) lung maturity — non-invasive alternative: quantusFLM (ultrasound texture analysis of the fetal lung; sensitivity 74-86%, specificity 87-89%; data in PROM are more limited), useful when the timing of delivery is uncertain. Methylene blue: used in the past; now contraindicated (see below). Methylene blue CONTRAINDICATED for intra-amniotic use — teratogenic; causes neonatal jejunal/ileal atresia, severe hyperbilirubinemia, fetal methemoglobinemia, and hemolysis. Safe alternatives: indigo carmine or fluorescein. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Alao AI et al. Arch Gynecol Obstet 2023;307(2):447-452. Microbiological analysis of amniotic fluid: Gram stain, culture (aerobes/anaerobes/Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma), amniotic fluid glucose (<14 mg/dL suggests intra-amniotic infection), leukocyte count.

novedades.texto: Gestational age Management Previable (<22-24 wk) Expectant management as an outpatient/inpatient; counseling on the risk of pulmonary hypoplasia, deformities, and stillbirth. Offer pregnancy termination or expectant management to all (SMFM #71, GRADE 1C). No tocolysis. Latency antibiotics may be considered from 20⁰/⁷ to 23⁶/⁷ (2C) and are recommended from 24⁰/⁷ (1B). Corticosteroids and MgSO4 only once neonatal resuscitation is planned (1B). Inform of the higher maternal risk with expectant management: morbidity 60.2% vs 33% and severe morbidity 12% vs 5% (ACOG 2025). Preterm, remote from term (24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ wk) Expectant inpatient management; complete course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone/dexamethasone); magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if delivery is imminent and GA<32 wk; mandatory latency antibiotic prophylaxis; tocolysis contraindicated or limited to 48h to complete corticosteroid treatment (if no infection). Late preterm (34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ wk) ACOG PB 217: expectant management or proceed to delivery (induction or cesarean as indicated). PPROMT (Lancet 2016): no difference in neonatal sepsis (2% vs 3%); immediate delivery had more respiratory distress (8% vs 5%) and more cesareans (26% vs 19%); expectant management had more hemorrhage and intrapartum fever. Expectant management until 37 weeks only if there are no signs of infection + close monitoring. At term (≥37⁰/⁷ wk) Induction (oxytocin or misoprostol if the cervix is unfavorable) within 12-24h to reduce the risk of intrauterine infection. novedades.texto: “Triple I” (Intrauterine Inflammation, Infection or both) is the modern term proposed by the 2015 NICHD workshop and adopted by ACOG/SMFM; it replaces “clinical chorioamnionitis” (classic Gibbs 1982 criteria: fever ≥37.8 °C + ≥2 signs; many guidelines use ≥38.0 °C). Definition in ACOG Committee Opinion 712 (2017) Category Criterion Suspected intra-amniotic infection (Triple I) — highest priority Maternal temperature ≥39.0 °C isolated, or 38.0-38.9 °C sustained (confirmed on repeat measurement at 30 min) plus 1 additional factor: maternal leukocytosis, purulent cervical drainage, or fetal tachycardia. Isolated maternal fever Temperature 38.0-38.9 °C without other factors, whether persistent or not. Management of Triple I: broad-spectrum antibiotics, delivery, and maternal resuscitation. In PROM, monitoring uses the same obstetric qSOFA (SBP <90, RR ≥25, altered mental status) used in the sepsis module; ≥2 points = high risk of deterioration. novedades.texto: Direct features (endometrial tissue in the myometrium): myometrial cysts · hyperechogenic islands · echogenic subendometrial lines and buds. Indirect features (effect on the myometrium): globular uterus · asymmetrical wall thickening · fan-shaped shadowing · translesional vascularity · irregular junctional zone · interrupted junctional zone. Diagnosis: at least one direct feature confirms adenomyosis. Indirect features only: inconclusive; MRI if it changes management. Revised MUSA 2022 advises against diagnosing by junctional zone thickness on ultrasound (the 12 mm cut-off was withdrawn). Report: location (anterior, posterior, fundal, lateral), pattern (diffuse, focal or adenomyoma), layers involved and extent (<25 %, 25–50 %, >50 % of uterine volume). Management: asymptomatic, no treatment. Symptomatic: LNG-IUS, dienogest or combined hormonal contraception, NSAIDs; if no response, GnRH analogues, embolization or selected adenomyomectomy; hysterectomy when childbearing is complete. Wish for pregnancy: refer to reproductive medicine. Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN (Uterus).

novedades.titulo: Infertile couple workup algorithm — Next step by results
novedades.fuentes: WHO 2025 · ASRM 2026 · ESHRE 2023 · AUA/ASRM 2024 · ASRM 2021 (tubal surgery) · RCPI 2023
novedades.texto: CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO 2025, ASRM 2026, ESHRE 2023, AUA/ASRM 2024, ASRM 2021, RCPI 2023. Step 1 — Basic workup in parallel: semen analysis · ovulation (cycle pattern and, if needed, mid-luteal progesterone) · transvaginal ultrasound with AFC · tubal patency (HSG or HyCoSy/HyFoSy) · AMH as appropriate · chlamydia serology as tubal triage (ESHRE). Step 2 — Management by finding: Azoospermia: urology/andrology; FSH, volume and pH; genetics (karyotype, Y microdeletions, CFTR as appropriate); surgical sperm retrieval + ICSI or donor sperm. Male factor by TMSC (CaVeSal® suggestion): >3–5 M → IUI · 1–3 M → IVF · <1 M → ICSI. Bilateral tubal obstruction: IVF/ICSI. Hydrosalpinx: salpingectomy or proximal occlusion before IVF (ASRM 2021). Unilateral: individualize. Anovulation by cause: PMOS → letrozole (first line) · hyperprolactinemia → dopamine agonist · thyroid dysfunction → correct · hypogonadotropic hypogonadism → gonadotropins or pulsatile GnRH · premature ovarian insufficiency → counseling, oocyte donation. Intracavitary pathology (polyp, submucous fibroid, septum, synechiae): hysteroscopy. Cervical factor or sexual dysfunction: IUI (RCPI 2023). The postcoital test is not recommended (ASRM 2026). Low reserve at ≥35 years: do not delay; refer to assisted reproduction. Unexplained infertility (all normal): good prognosis → expectant (WHO 2025: rather than unstimulated IUI; ESHRE 2023); poor prognosis → IUI with ovarian stimulation for 3–6 cycles → IVF. Infections: chlamydia and gonorrhea by risk, treating both partners. Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma: no guideline (ASRM, ESHRE, WHO) supports routine testing in infertility; only with clinical findings (cervicitis, urethritis, PID). See "Chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium and Ureaplasma". Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN (Couple workup): pressing Calculate shows the next step.

novedades.fuentes: ASRM Committee Opinion (2026) · ASRM (2021) · WHO 2025 · ESHRE 2023
novedades.texto: When to evaluate: no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (<35 years), after 6 months (≥35 years) and immediately after 40 or with a known cause (oligo/amenorrhea, endometriosis, PID, pelvic surgery, chemo- or radiotherapy, known male factor). Evaluate both partners in parallel. Pillars: (1) Ovarian — regular 21–35-day cycles suggest ovulation; with irregular cycles confirm with mid-luteal progesterone (WHO 2025) and look for the cause with a hormonal profile (FSH, estradiol, prolactin, TSH, androgens). Reserve with AMH and AFC. (2) Tubal — HSG or HyCoSy/HyFoSy (equivalent); with high risk (chlamydia or PID, endometriosis, pelvic surgery, ectopic) consider laparoscopy with chromopertubation. (3) Uterine — transvaginal ultrasound, ideally 3D; suspected intracavitary lesion → sonohysterography or hysteroscopy. Not routine (ASRM 2026): postcoital test, TSH and prolactin without clinical indication, thrombophilia testing and karyotype. Next step by results: see "Infertile couple workup algorithm". novedades.texto: Branch 1 — Patient on GLP-1/GIP treatment who is NOT seeking pregnancy (or has not yet decided): Active contraceptive counseling from the start of treatment, even if she previously had anovulation due to PMOS (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide) — fertility can recover before the patient notices. Prefer non-oral methods (LARC, injectable, patch, ring), especially with tirzepatide; if she uses an oral method, add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation (see the Contraception during tirzepatide guide). Branch 2 — Patient who IS seeking pregnancy (preconception planning): Washout by molecule before attempting to conceive (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide) — semaglutide ≥2 months, tirzepatide ≥1 month (European/UK label), extended-release exenatide ≥3 months; no validated interval for liraglutide, dulaglutide, short-acting exenatide or lixisenatide; retatrutide does not apply, as it is not approved. Reassess baseline metabolic management (metformin, myo-inositol) in a preconception context, not a weight-loss one (see the Metformin in pregnancy and Myo-inositol guides). Preconception folic acid according to risk level (see the Preconception screening and folic acid guide). Branch 3 — Inadvertent pregnancy already confirmed during GLP-1/GIP use: Stop the drug immediately. Reassess the metabolic plan in a pregnancy context, not a weight-loss one (see the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide). Discuss the available evidence with the patient — reassuring regarding malformations, more mixed regarding gestational weight gain/gestational diabetes/hypertension (see the same guide) — without creating unwarranted alarm or false reassurance. 5 key messages for counseling: GLP-1/GIP-slowed gastric emptying can reduce absorption of oral contraceptives — discuss it proactively, not reactively. Fertility recovery from weight loss can occur before the patient notices the menstrual change. Preconception washout varies by molecule — there is no single rule for "the GLP-1s." Facing an inadvertent pregnancy, stopping the drug is the immediate step — evidence on malformations is reassuring so far, but evidence on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes is more mixed and warrants active pregnancy follow-up, not just reassurance. The real teratogen in diabetes is uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not the drug itself — do not stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan.

novedades.titulo: Threatened preterm labor (TPL) — Diagnosis and tocolysis
novedades.fuentes: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 171 (2016, reaffirmed 2022) · NICE NG25 (2019, updated 2022) · FIGO Recommendations on Preterm Birth (2021)
novedades.texto: Diagnosis: regular uterine dynamics (≥4/20min) + cervical changes, 22-36+6 wk. TVUS: CL >30mm rules out TPL · CL <25mm high risk · 20-30mm → biomarkers (fetal fibronectin/PAMG-1). Tocolysis (22/24-33+6 wk): Nifedipine (1st line) loading dose 10-20mg q20min → maintenance q6-8h · Atosiban (NICE/RCOG) · Indomethacin (before wk 32, do not combine with MgSO4 or nifedipine).

novedades.fuentes: AACE/ACE · Endocrine Society · SURMOUNT/STEP · Austin GO, et al. Front Mol Biosci 2023;10:1170181 · Davies M, et al. Lancet 2021;397(10278):971-984 · Rubino D, et al. JAMA 2021;325(14):1414-1425 (STEP 4) · Aronne LJ, et al. JAMA 2024;331(1):38-48 (SURMOUNT-4) · Castaneda R, et al. The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128. doi:10.1016/S3050-5038(25)00145-1 · Wilding JPH, et al. Diabetes Obes Metab 2022;24(8):1553-1564 (STEP 1 extension)
novedades.texto: Semaglutide 0.25→2.4mg/wk. Tirzepatide 2.5→10-15mg/wk. Indication: BMI≥30, or ≥27+comorbidity. ⚠️ "Ozempic babies" (restores ovulation), reduces OCP efficacy, stop before trying to conceive according to the molecule (semaglutide ≥2 months; tirzepatide ≥1 month per the European/UK label; see Preconception washout by molecule guide), risk of sarcopenia. Non-response rates (<5% weight loss) by pivotal trial: STEP-1 (semaglutide 2.4mg, non-diabetic adults) 13.6% · STEP-TEENS (semaglutide 2.4mg, adolescents with excess-weight comorbidity) 27% · SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide 15mg, non-diabetic adults) 9% · STEP-2 (semaglutide 2.4mg, diabetic adults) 31.2% — response is consistently lower in patients with concomitant type 2 diabetes, a point to anticipate when counseling on expectations. Maintaining weight loss requires continuing the medication (STEP 4 with semaglutide and SURMOUNT-4 with tirzepatide): in both trials, patients who, on reaching a weight-loss plateau, were randomized to continue the drug maintained or further deepened their weight loss, while those switched to placebo progressively regained weight over the remaining follow-up — obesity behaves here as a chronic condition requiring sustained treatment, not as a short course with a permanent outcome. Figures: STEP 4 (Rubino 2021), weeks 20-68: −7.9% with semaglutide vs. +6.9% with placebo; SURMOUNT-4 (Aronne, JAMA 2024;331(1):38-48), weeks 36-88: −5.5% with tirzepatide vs. +14.0% with placebo. STEP 1 extension (Wilding, Diabetes Obes Metab 2022; n=327): after −17.3% at week 68, stopping led to regain of 11.6 percentage points by week 120, about two-thirds of the weight lost. GLP-1/GIP + hormone therapy in the climacteric (retrospective cohort, Mayo Clinic): Castaneda et al. (The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128), in 120 postmenopausal women with overweight/obesity on tirzepatide (40 on HRT vs. 80 without, propensity-matched), reported that at 15 months HRT users had 35% greater total body weight loss than non-users, along with additional cardiometabolic improvements in both groups. ⚠️ This is retrospective matched-cohort evidence, not a randomized trial — it suggests a possible synergy but does not establish causality, nor does it by itself change the indication for HRT, which should be decided on its own criteria (see the MRS Scale and HRT guide). Note: the preliminary figure presented at the ENDO 2025 congress (~17% vs. 14%) differs from the final Lancet publication — this guide uses the final published figure (35% relative difference), not the preliminary congress figure.

novedades.titulo: Cervical cancer — Screening and management algorithm (ASCCP)
novedades.fuentes: ASCCP 2019 (Perkins et al., 2020) · J Low Genit Tract Dis 2024;28:3-6 · ASCCP enduring guidelines 2024-2025
novedades.texto: Age: <21 none · 21-29 Pap every 3 years · 30-65 primary hrHPV every 5 years (preferred), co-test every 5 or Pap every 3 · >65 stop if adequate prior screening. HIV or immunosuppression: special schedule. Management by result: negative HPV or co-test → 5 years · HPV 16/18 → colposcopy even with NILM · other HPV + NILM → repeat in 1 year · ASC-US + HPV negative → 3 years · ASC-US + HPV positive → colposcopy (<25 years: cytology in 1 year) · LSIL ≥25 → colposcopy (<25: cytology in 1 year) · ASC-H → colposcopy always · HSIL ≥25 → expedited excision or colposcopy (<25: colposcopy) · AGC → colposcopy + endocervical sampling + endometrial sampling if ≥35 or at risk · AIS → diagnostic excision · carcinoma → biopsy and gynecologic oncology. 2024-2025 updates: p16/Ki-67 dual stain for HPV-positive triage (positive → colposcopy; negative → HPV in 1 year). Self-collected vaginal HPV accepted: 16/18 → colposcopy; other types → clinician-collected sample for cytology; negative → repeat in 3 years. Extended genotyping: use the ASCCP app for exact risk. Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN (Breast, cervix and endometrium). ASCCP enduring guidelines.

novedades.fuentes: FIGO 2018 (Bhatla N et al. IJGO 2019;145:129-135) · ESGO-ESTRO-ESP 2023
novedades.texto: I confined to the cervix: IA1 invasion ≤3 mm · IA2 >3–5 mm · IB1 ≤2 cm · IB2 >2–4 cm · IB3 >4 cm. II beyond the uterus, not lower third of vagina or pelvic wall: IIA1 upper vagina, tumor ≤4 cm · IIA2 >4 cm · IIB parametria. III IIIA lower third of vagina · IIIB pelvic wall or hydronephrosis · IIIC1 pelvic nodes · IIIC2 para-aortic nodes (r imaging, p pathology; nodes define IIIC regardless of tumor size). IV IVA bladder or rectal mucosa (biopsy) · IVB distant metastasis. Management (ESGO 2023): pelvic MRI mandatory; PET-CT or CT for IB3 or higher (except IIA1) or suspicious nodes. IA1 without LVSI: conization or simple hysterectomy. IA1 with LVSI or IA2: add sentinel node. IB1–IIA1: radical hysterectomy with pelvic nodes, open approach; radical trachelectomy if IB1 and fertility desired. IB3 and IIA2–IVA: platinum chemoradiation plus brachytherapy. IVB: systemic. Always gynecologic oncology. Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN (Oncology).

novedades.fuentes: FIGO 2023 (Berek JS et al. IJGO 2023;162:383-394) · ESGO-ESTRO-ESP 2025 (Lancet Oncol 2025) · ESGO/ESHRE/ESGE 2023
novedades.texto: Histotypes: non-aggressive = grade 1–2 endometrioid. Aggressive = grade 3 endometrioid, serous, clear cell, undifferentiated, mixed, mesonephric-like, gastrointestinal mucinous, carcinosarcoma. I (uterus, non-aggressive without substantial LVSI): IA1 endometrium or polyp · IA2 invasion <50 % · IA3 low-grade limited to uterus and ovary (unilateral, no rupture, <50 %, no substantial LVSI) · IB ≥50 % · IC aggressive limited to endometrium or polyp. II IIA cervical stroma (non-aggressive) · IIB substantial LVSI (non-aggressive) · IIC aggressive with myometrial invasion. III IIIA1 ovary or tube · IIIA2 serosa · IIIB1 vagina or parametria · IIIB2 pelvic peritoneum · IIIC1 pelvic nodes (i micro, ii macro) · IIIC2 para-aortic (i, ii). IV IVA bladder or bowel mucosa · IVB abdominal peritoneum beyond the pelvis · IVC distant metastasis. Molecular group in I–II: POLEmut → IAm POLEmut · p53abn with myometrial invasion → IICm p53abn · MMRd and NSMP are recorded. In III–IV the stage does not change. Management: molecular classification in all; MMRd → Lynch testing. Pelvic MRI or expert ultrasound; CT if high risk. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and sentinel node. IAm POLEmut and low risk: no adjuvant therapy. IICm p53abn: chemotherapy ± radiotherapy. III–IVA: surgery plus systemic therapy (immunotherapy especially in MMRd) ± radiotherapy. IVB–IVC: systemic. Fertility preservation: low-grade IA1 in a referral center. Always gynecologic oncology. Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN (Oncology).

novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® summary based on AJCC 8th ed. (anatomic and prognostic stage) · NCCN · ESMO 2024
novedades.texto: T (size): Tis in situ · T1 up to 2 cm · T2 more than 2 and up to 5 cm · T3 more than 5 cm · T4 chest wall or skin (includes inflammatory carcinoma). N (nodes): N0 none · N1 mobile ipsilateral axillary · N2 fixed axillary or internal mammary · N3 infraclavicular, supraclavicular or axillary with internal mammary. M: M0 no metastasis · M1 distant metastasis. Prognostic stage: AJCC 8th ed. adds grade, estrogen and progesterone receptors, HER2 and, when available, genomic assay; the stage may go up or down versus the anatomic stage. For the exact stage, use the AJCC manual. Management: asymptomatic stage I–II: no routine staging imaging. Stage III, symptoms or abnormal labs: contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus bone scan, or PET-CT. Breast MRI in selected cases. Genetic counseling by criteria (BRCA). Treatment by a multidisciplinary breast team. CaVeSal® original summary; does not reproduce AJCC tables.

novedades.fuentes: FIGO 2014 (Prat J. IJGO 2014;124:1-5) · ESGO-ESMO-ESP 2024 (Ann Oncol 2024;35:248-266)
novedades.texto: I ovaries or tubes: IA one · IB both · IC1 surgical spill · IC2 rupture before surgery or surface tumor · IC3 malignant cells in ascites or washings. II pelvis: IIA uterus or tubes · IIB other pelvic tissues. III IIIA1 retroperitoneal nodes only (i ≤10 mm, ii >10 mm) · IIIA2 microscopic extrapelvic peritoneum · IIIB macroscopic ≤2 cm · IIIC >2 cm (includes liver and spleen capsule). IV IVA pleural effusion with positive cytology · IVB parenchymal or extra-abdominal metastases (includes inguinal nodes). Management (ESGO-ESMO-ESP 2024): contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis; CA-125 and CEA. Germline and somatic BRCA in high-grade non-mucinous of any stage, HRD in stage III–IV BRCA wild-type, genetic counseling. I–II: complete staging surgery; fertility-sparing in selected cases; adjuvant platinum except low-grade IA–IB. III–IV: primary cytoreduction to no residual disease or neoadjuvant chemotherapy and interval surgery; maintenance by BRCA/HRD (PARP inhibitors, bevacizumab). Imaging alone does not decide resectability. Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN (Oncology).

novedades.fuentes: USPSTF (2023) · ACOG CO 762 (2019)
novedades.texto: Basic labs + serologies + Pap/mammogram as appropriate. Folic acid: standard 400mcg/day · high risk 4 mg/day (ACOG/CDC) or 5 mg/day (NICE/RCOG) up to wk 12 (prior NTD in the woman or partner, diabetes, obesity, epilepsy or anticonvulsants). MTHFR: standard folic acid at the same dose (CDC). It is the only form of folate shown to prevent neural tube defects; methylfolate (5-MTHF) does not replace it. MTHFR testing is not recommended (ACMG 2013, reaffirmed in 2020). Paraguay context (MSPyBS): the official public health communication from Paraguay's Ministry of Public Health and Welfare (MSPyBS) recommends 0.5mg (500mcg)/day as the standard preconception/gestational folic acid dose — slightly higher than the international 400mcg standard cited above, without changing the high-risk dose (4-5mg/day) in the risk scenarios already described. The MSPyBS Manual de Cuidados Perinatales (Resolución S.G. N.º 1078/2022, already cited elsewhere in this guide section for the PBF re-evaluation window) structures the preconception visit as "traffic-light" (semáforo), i.e. tiered by risk level — confirmed that this scheme exists in the official document.

novedades.titulo: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraception
novedades.fuentes: CDC US MEC 2024 · WHO MEC 6th ed. (2025) · SIC 2025 · FSRH (2017, amended 2023)
novedades.texto: Categories: 1 no restriction · 2 advantages generally outweigh risks · 3 risks generally outweigh advantages (only if no other method is available or acceptable, with follow-up) · 4 unacceptable risk, do not use. With several conditions, the highest category applies. Some conditions have one category for initiation and another for continuation. Cat 4 for combined methods (US MEC 2024): breastfeeding or postpartum under 21 days; smoker aged 35 or older with 15 or more cigarettes per day; BP 160/100 or higher or vascular disease; prior VTE with high recurrence risk (no anticoagulation or prophylactic dose); known thrombophilia; major surgery with prolonged immobilization; ischemic heart disease; stroke; complicated valvular disease; peripartum cardiomyopathy (under 6 months or moderately or severely impaired function); SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies; migraine with aura; current breast cancer; decompensated cirrhosis; hepatocellular adenoma or carcinoma; chronic kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome or dialysis); sickle cell disease; transplant with graft failure. Cat 3 to 4 by severity: multiple cardiovascular risk factors, diabetes with end-organ damage or over 20 years' duration. Progestin-only: cat 4 with current breast cancer; cat 3 with past cancer and no disease for 5 years. The 3-monthly injectable (DMPA) is cat 3 with BP 160/100 or higher, vascular disease, ischemic heart disease, stroke, high-risk VTE, thrombophilia and diabetes with end-organ damage. IUD (copper and LNG), cat 4 for initiation: pregnancy, puerperal sepsis, immediately after septic abortion, current PID or purulent cervicitis, chlamydia or gonorrhea, distorted uterine cavity, unexplained bleeding before evaluation, cervical or endometrial cancer awaiting treatment, trophoblastic disease with intrauterine disease, pelvic tuberculosis. Differences with WHO 2025 (6th ed.): progestin injectables while breastfeeding under 6 weeks moved from cat 3 to 2 and can be offered immediately after delivery; nevirapine and ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors moved to cat 1 with all hormonal methods (US MEC 2024 keeps cat 2 or 3 for some); with PrEP all methods are cat 1; repeated emergency contraception in the same cycle is cat 1; inflammatory bowel disease was added. Over 40 (SIC consensus 2025): cardiovascular safety is the main factor. Estrogen-free methods do not increase venous or arterial risk. Among combined methods, EE/levonorgestrel, EE/norgestimate and natural estradiol increase VTE the least; EE 20 µg with drospirenone and natural estradiol do not increase arterial risk. Heavy bleeding, from most to least effective: LNG-IUD 52 mg, estradiol valerate/dienogest, ring, COC with EE 30-35 µg, progestin-only. COCs protect bone; the implant, progestin-only pill and LNG-IUD are neutral. When to stop contraception (FSRH): generally at 55. Non-hormonal method: 2 years of amenorrhea under 50 and 1 year at 50 or older. Combined and DMPA: until 50, then switch method. Implant, progestin-only pill or LNG-IUD with amenorrhea from age 50: if FSH is above 30 IU/L, stop after 1 more year. FSH is not useful on combined methods or MHT. MHT can be added to a non-combined method. Other data: tirzepatide may reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives; use a non-oral method or add a barrier for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (FDA label). The etonogestrel implant is approved for 5 years (ANMAT 2025).

novedades.fuentes: CLAP-PAHO/WHO
novedades.texto: Pregnancy lasts, on average, 280 days (40 weeks) from the first day of the LMP — 9 calendar months or 10 lunar months. Always expressed in completed weeks. Rules to estimate EDD: Wahl (LMP+10 days, -3 months) · Naegele (LMP+7 days, -3 months) · Pinard (last day of menstruation+10 days, -3 months; the least used). In the medical record the EDD is calculated with Naegele or Wahl and is always editable; Pinard appears only as a reference in this guide. Ultrasound correction: if it differs beyond the accepted margin, GA by ultrasound takes priority — the earlier the scan, the more reliable (maximum precision in the 1st trimester).

novedades.titulo: Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide — what the evidence shows
novedades.fuentes: Brown ME, et al. GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use During the Periconceptional Period, Ann Intern Med (2026) — target trial emulation, n=3,572 · D'Antonio F, et al. Periconceptional and early pregnancy exposure to GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists and obstetric/neonatal outcomes, Med (2026) — meta-analysis, n=2,118,215 · AJOG 2024 (review), PII S0002-9378(24)00864-0 · Uysal N, et al. Pregnancy outcomes following maternal GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2026;16:31416 · Liu X, et al. Periconceptional use of GLP-1 receptor agonists and the risk of major congenital malformations: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Endocr Connect. 2026;15(7). DOI 10.1530/EC-26-0280 · Maya J, et al. Gestational Weight Gain and Pregnancy Outcomes After GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Discontinuation. JAMA. 2025;334(24):2186-2196. DOI 10.1001/jama.2025.20951 · Pondugula N, et al. Gestational Weight Gain and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy With Prepregnancy and Early Pregnancy GLP-1RA Exposure. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;147(3):293-302. DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000005995
novedades.texto: Immediate management of an inadvertent pregnancy in a patient using GLP-1/GIP: Stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is confirmed — current evidence does not support continuing it during gestation, regardless of the duration of periconceptional exposure that has already occurred. Reassess the patient's overall metabolic management plan (glycemia, weight, possible metformin indication — see corresponding guide) now in the context of pregnancy, not of weight loss. There is no indication for pregnancy termination based solely on periconceptional GLP-1/GIP exposure — the conversation with the patient should be grounded in the available evidence (summarized below), which so far shows no consistent signal of harm. What the evidence shows (quick-reference summary, not a substitute for each study's methodological detail): Brown et al. (Ann Intern Med 2026, target trial emulation, n=3,572) found no significant increase in major congenital malformations associated with periconceptional exposure to GLP-1 agonists, using a design that emulates a randomized trial from observational data to reduce confounding by indication. Major congenital malformations: adjusted prevalence ratio 1.21 (95% CI 0.83-1.82); non-live birth: adjusted RR 1.09 (Ann Intern Med 2026;179(7):929-937). Wide intervals: a moderate effect cannot be excluded. D'Antonio et al. (Med 2026, large-scale meta-analysis, n=2,118,215) likewise found no consistent signal of increased risk of adverse obstetric/neonatal outcomes associated with periconceptional or early-pregnancy exposure to GLP-1/GIP agonists — this being the largest sample-size analysis available to date on the topic. The AJOG 2024 review (PII S0002-9378(24)00864-0) synthesizes the body of evidence available at that time in the same reassuring direction, although — like the rest of this literature — it is based predominantly on observational studies rather than randomized trials specifically designed to assess reproductive safety. ⚠️ All of this evidence is observational (cohorts, target trial emulation, cohort meta-analyses) — absence of a harm signal is not equivalent to definitive evidence of safety, and it does not change the recommendation to stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is recognized, nor the recommendation to respect the preconception washout by molecule when pregnancy is planned (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide). Malformations — additional meta-analysis (Uysal et al., Sci Rep 2026;16:31416): across 7 cohort studies with over 40,000 exposed pregnancies, there was no significant signal for congenital malformations overall (OR 1.11; 95% CI 0.82-1.51) nor for major malformations with first-trimester exposure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.73-2.65). An isolated significant signal was found for urinary malformations (OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.05-1.47), based on unadjusted data from only 2 studies — the authors themselves attribute it most likely to residual confounding (underlying maternal diabetes/obesity), not a direct teratogenic effect. No increased signal was found for stillbirth, spontaneous abortion, small for gestational age, or preterm birth. Major congenital malformations — largest sample-size meta-analysis available to date (Liu X, et al. Endocrine Connections 2026;15(7). DOI 10.1530/EC-26-0280): across 6 studies (1 prospective + 5 retrospective) with 286,599 women, of whom 43,577 had periconceptional GLP-1RA exposure, there was no significant difference in the risk of major congenital malformations between exposed and unexposed women (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.96-1.08). No significant signal was found either for preterm birth (RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.80-1.49), large for gestational age (RR 2.31; 95% CI 0.56-9.44), small for gestational age (RR 0.71; 95% CI 0.39-1.27), or stillbirth (RR 1.16; 95% CI 0.24-5.69) — these last three have very wide confidence intervals due to low event numbers, and should be read as "insufficient statistical power to detect a risk if one existed," not as "no risk." The authors themselves note that, given the observational design and limited number of exposed pregnancies, these findings should not be interpreted as proof of safety. Gestational weight gain and complications after stopping the drug (Maya J, et al. JAMA 2025;334(24):2186-2196 — retrospective cohort, Mass General Brigham, n=448 exposed vs. 1,344 unexposed, matched by propensity score 1:3, 84% with obesity): exposure to GLP-1/GIP between 3 years before and 90 days after conception was associated with greater gestational weight gain (mean 13.7kg vs. 10.5kg; difference +3.3kg; 95% CI 2.3-4.2; p<0.001), a higher risk of excess gestational weight gain (65% vs. 49%; RR 1.32; 95% CI 1.19-1.47), of preterm delivery (17% vs. 13%; RR 1.34; 95% CI 1.06-1.69), of gestational diabetes (20% vs. 15%; RR 1.30; 95% CI 1.01-1.68), and of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (46% vs. 36%; RR 1.29; 95% CI 1.12-1.49) — with no difference in birth length, large/small for gestational age, or cesarean delivery. ⚠️ Unlike Liu et al. (above), which looks for a malformation signal, this cohort looks at the pregnant patient's own metabolic/hypertensive outcomes after periconceptional exposure — a different, and to some extent contrasting, perspective to the reassurance conveyed by Imbroane et al. 2025 (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide): "no malformation signal" does not equal "no maternal risk at all." Cohort composed mostly of women with obesity — limits generalization to a non-obese population. Gestational weight gain and hypertensive disorders — independent cohort (Pondugula N, et al. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;147(3):293-302. DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000005995): a retrospective cohort distinct from Maya et al. (Yale, n=243 exposed up to 1 year before pregnancy — 103 for pregestational diabetes, 140 for weight management — vs. 175 and 200 unexposed, respectively). Found no association between GLP-1RA exposure and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in either cohort (pregestational diabetes: adjusted OR 0.72; 95% CI 0.42-1.25 · weight management: adjusted OR 0.83; 95% CI 0.45-1.52). There was also no association with gestational weight gain in the pregestational diabetes cohort; in the weight-management cohort, exposure was associated with a lower likelihood of gestational weight gain below recommendations (adjusted OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.18-0.78) — the authors interpret this as a possible rebound weight gain after stopping the drug, not as excess weight gain. ⚠️ Important attribution note: the figures of 65% vs. 49% excess weight gain, 20% vs. 15% gestational diabetes, and 46% vs. 36% hypertensive disorders (above) belong to Maya et al., not to this study — these are two independent cohorts with different findings (Pondugula et al. reports no hypertensive-disorder signal; Maya et al. does).

novedades.texto: Careful history/exam to choose studies. Essential female evaluation in parallel. Counseling on tobacco+STIs. Document outcomes. Psychosocial support. Key points for the workup (WHO 2025, 40 recommendations): ovulation by mid-luteal progesterone rather than serial ultrasound tracking · tubal patency by HSG or HyCoSy · abnormal semen analysis: repeat at 11 weeks or later · unexplained infertility: expectant management rather than unstimulated IUI · PMOS with anovulation: letrozole as first line. Next step by results: see "Infertile couple workup algorithm".
